At which Olympics did women compete for the first time?
Twenty-two women took part among nearly a thousand men, in golf, tennis, croquet and sailing, and several did not know they were in the Olympics at all.
The 1904 Olympics were awarded to Chicago and then taken away. Which city got them?
St. Louis was staging a World's Fair and threatened to run a rival sports festival, so the Games were simply moved to it.
Rome gave up the 1908 Olympics after Mount Vesuvius erupted. Which city took them on?
The Italian money went to rebuilding Naples instead, and London put the Games together in under two years.
At which Games did an Olympic flame first burn in the stadium?
It burned in the tower by the marathon gate; the torch relay from Olympia was only invented eight years later.
At which Games was the Olympic flag flown for the first time?
Germany, Austria, Hungary, Bulgaria and Turkey were not invited to those first Games after the war.
In which year was Olympic competition shown on television for the first time?
Pictures from Berlin were piped to about twenty-five viewing halls around the city; nobody had a set at home.
Tokyo gave up the 1940 Olympics. Which capital was to take over before they were cancelled?
The stadium was built and the tickets printed; the war took the Games and the city had to wait another twelve years.
At the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, one sport was contested 15,000 km away in Stockholm. Which?
Australian quarantine law would not let foreign horses in, so the riders went to Sweden five months before the rest of the Games.
Who won the 1960 Olympic marathon through the streets of Rome, running barefoot?
An Ethiopian palace guard, he won again in Tokyo four years later, in shoes, forty days after an appendix operation.
Which Olympic host opened a new high-speed railway days before the Games began?
The Tokaido Shinkansen cut the journey to Osaka almost in half and was built largely to move Olympic crowds.
Waldi the dachshund was the first official mascot of which Olympics?
West Germany wanted something cheerful after 1936 and chose a rainbow-striped sausage dog; every Games has had a mascot since.
Which Olympic host city took thirty years to pay off its main stadium?
The debt from 1976 was cleared only in 2006, and locals had nicknamed the unfinished tower the Big Owe.
Some teams at the 1980 Moscow Olympics marched under which flag instead of their own?
Sixty-odd countries stayed away over Afghanistan, and several that came would not show their own colours.
How was the cauldron lit at the opening of the 1992 Barcelona Olympics?
A Paralympic archer shot it over the rim in front of 65,000 people, and the arrow landed in the stadium moat.
Which sport returned to the Olympic programme in 2016 after 112 years away?
It had last been played in 1904; several of the world's best players skipped Rio anyway, citing the Zika virus.
At the 2004 Athens Olympics one event was staged in the ancient stadium at Olympia. Which?
It was thrown on grass with no seating, the crowd sitting on the banks as spectators did two and a half thousand years ago.
Which city was the first to host both a Summer and a Winter Olympics?
It had the Summer Games in 2008 and the Winter Games in 2022, which were run almost entirely on artificial snow.
Which sport made its Olympic debut at Garmisch-Partenkirchen in 1936?
Ski instructors were ruled professionals and barred, so Switzerland and Austria boycotted the event in protest.
The 1952 Winter Olympic flame was not lit in Greece. Where was it lit?
It was lit in Morgedal, in the fireplace of the house where Sondre Norheim, the father of modern skiing, grew up.
Which Winter Olympics were the first at which drug and sex tests were carried out?
They were also the first Winter Games broadcast in colour, so viewers could finally tell the teams apart.
Colorado voters refused to pay for the 1976 Winter Olympics. Which city took them instead?
Denver is the only host in Olympic history to have handed the Games back after winning them.
Which American village of a few thousand people has hosted two Winter Olympics?
It staged the Games in 1932 and 1980, more than New York, Chicago and Boston have managed between them.
Bobsleigh was dropped from one Winter Olympics for lack of entries. Which Games?
Only nine countries entered, so the organisers refused to build a track at all, the only Winter Games without the sport since 1924.
After which Games did the Winter Olympics stop sharing a year with the Summer ones?
The next Winter Games came after only two years, to put the two Olympics on alternating even years.
Which sport was added to the Winter Olympics at Nagano in 1998?
The first halfpipe champion lost his gold over a cannabis test and got it back when it turned out the drug was not on the banned list.
Which Winter Olympic host was so warm that snow had to be brought in by lorry and helicopter?
It is the warmest city ever to have staged a Winter Games, and the freestyle hill was built on straw bales under trucked-in snow.
The bobsleigh track and ski jumps of which Winter Olympics stand in ruins today?
They were shelled during the siege of the city eight years after the Games, and the bob run is now covered in graffiti.
At which Winter Olympics did North and South Korea put out a joint women's ice hockey team?
They also marched in together under a unification flag, and the combined team lost all five of its matches.
The 1930 champions refused to come back and defend the trophy in 1934. Who were they?
It was still angry that most European teams had not bothered to sail to Montevideo four years earlier.
Which was the first country to win two football World Cups in a row?
It won in 1934 and 1938, and nobody repeated the double until Brazil in 1958 and 1962.
The 1950 football World Cup had no final match. How was the winner decided?
Brazil needed only a draw in the last game and lost 2-1 to Uruguay in front of some two hundred thousand people.
Which team was unbeaten for four years, beat its opponents 8-3 in the group, and still lost the 1954 final?
West Germany won the final 3-2 in the rain in Bern, and Hungary never won a World Cup at all.
How old was Pele when he scored twice in the World Cup final of 1958?
He is still the youngest man to have played in a World Cup final, let alone won one, and he cried on the pitch afterwards.
The World Cup trophy was stolen in England in 1966. What found it a week later?
A mongrel called Pickles sniffed out a newspaper parcel under a hedge in south London; he got a year's free dog food.
Why did Brazil get to keep the original World Cup trophy outright in 1970?
The solid gold cup was stolen from a cabinet in Rio in 1983 and has never been found; it was probably melted down.
In the 1974 final the Netherlands scored before a German had touched the ball. Who won the match?
Johan Neeskens converted a penalty after eighty seconds, and the Dutch did not score again; they lost 2-1.
Which player returned from a two-year betting ban to win the 1982 World Cup golden boot?
He had scored nothing in the first four matches and then scored six in three, including a hat-trick against Brazil.
Against which team did Maradona score the Hand of God goal in 1986?
Four minutes later he beat half the same team on a sixty-metre run to score what a FIFA poll called the goal of the century.
Which country won the football World Cup in 1990 and stopped existing under that name months later?
The final was in July and the country was reunified in October, so the title is held by a state that no longer exists.
Which was the first World Cup final to be decided by a penalty shoot-out?
Roberto Baggio put the last kick over the bar in Pasadena after a goalless two hours in brutal heat.
Which favourite played the 1998 World Cup final hours after a convulsive fit at the team hotel?
He was taken off the team sheet and then put back on; Brazil lost 3-0 and he said afterwards he remembered almost nothing.
Which football World Cup was shared between two host countries?
Japan and South Korea were both bidding and neither would give way, so FIFA gave it to the pair of them.
Spain won the 2010 World Cup having scored how many goals in the whole tournament?
That is the fewest by any champion; four of its knockout matches finished 1-0, including the final.
Germany beat the hosts 7-1 in a 2014 World Cup semi-final. What do Brazilians call that match?
The name echoes the Maracanazo of 1950, the other home defeat Brazilians have never got over.
Croatia reached the 2018 World Cup final with a population of roughly how many?
It is the smallest country to reach a final since Uruguay in 1950, and it played three straight extra-time knockout matches to get there.
Which ground hosted the World Cup finals of both 1970 and 1986?
No other stadium had hosted two finals until the Maracana did it in 2014, 64 years after its first.
Zidane was sent off in the 2006 World Cup final, the last match of his career. What for?
Italy won the shoot-out, and he had still been voted the best player of the tournament a day earlier.
Who won the first Formula One drivers' championship, in 1950?
He beat his own Alfa Romeo team-mate Fangio by three points, and Fangio then won five of the next seven titles.
Juan Manuel Fangio won his five world titles driving for how many different makes of car?
Alfa Romeo, Maserati, Mercedes and Ferrari; no champion since has won titles with more than two different marques.
Which driver won nine Formula One Grands Prix in a row across the 1952 and 1953 seasons?
No one matched the run for sixty years, and he was killed testing a sports car at Monza in 1955, aged 36.
Which driver has won a Formula One world title in a car bearing his own name?
He did it in 1966, in a car his own firm built, and he is still the only one; he was 40 years old.
Which driver was awarded the Formula One world title of 1970 after his death?
He was killed at Monza with four races of the season left, and nobody caught his points total.
Which champion led the campaign for seat belts, barriers and medical cars in Formula One?
He reckoned a driver who raced through his era had about a two-in-three chance of being killed, and he went to a great many funerals.
Niki Lauda pulled out of the last race of 1976 in the rain in Japan. Who took the title by a point?
Lauda had been dragged from a burning car at the Nurburgring six weeks earlier and was back racing in 42 days.
Which Formula One champion was nicknamed the Professor?
He won on tyre wear and arithmetic rather than lap records, and often finished a race with a car that still looked clean.
Ayrton Senna took 65 pole positions. In how many Grand Prix starts?
That is a pole in more than two races out of five, a rate nobody in the history of the sport has come near.
Michael Schumacher was struck out of the 1997 standings for driving into a rival. Who became champion?
The collision at Jerez put them both off the track, but Schumacher's car stopped and his rival's carried on to finish third.
Which driver won five Formula One world titles in a row?
From 2000 to 2004; in 2002 he won eleven of the seventeen races and had the championship settled by July.
What did Nico Rosberg do five days after winning the 2016 Formula One title?
He had spent ten years trying to beat Lewis Hamilton, said he had nothing left to prove, and never raced again at 31.
Which Formula One champion gave every one of his racing cars a girl's name?
Kate, Luscious Liz, Hungry Heidi and Suzie among them, and he talked to the car on the grid before the start.
In which sport did Verner Weckman win Finland's first ever Olympic gold, in 1908?
Finland was still a Grand Duchy of Russia, and its athletes were allowed no flag of their own at those Games.
At which Games did Finland win fifteen Olympic golds, more than at any other?
A country of three million took fifteen golds and 34 medals in all, and finished near the top of the medal table.
How many Olympic gold medals has Finland won in all, summer and winter together?
101 came at the Summer Games and 45 at the Winter, and more than half the summer ones were won before 1940.
When did Finland last win an Olympic gold medal in athletics?
Heli Rantanen's javelin was the last of them, and the country that once owned the distance races has not thrown or run for gold since.
Hannes Kolehmainen won three Olympic titles on the track in 1912. Which did he add in 1920?
He won it by thirteen seconds over a course measured at 42.75 km, and it was said he had run Finland onto the map.
Which Finn won four golds in Paris in 1924 and another in Amsterdam in 1928?
He had emigrated to New York as a young man and only took up serious running at 25, after watching a Finnish club meeting there.
In which sport did Clas Thunberg win five Olympic golds for Finland in the 1920s?
He had never raced abroad before his first Games, and all five golds came after he had turned thirty.
Which Finn won the Olympic javelin gold in 1932 and broke the world record ten times?
The tower of the Helsinki Olympic Stadium was built to 72.71 metres because that was the length of his best throw.
Which Finn won the 1928 Olympic decathlon, having trained alone on his own farm with no coach?
He set a world record in winning it and went on competing between the harvests at Hauho for another eight years.
In the 1932 Olympic steeplechase final the lap counter lost count. How far did the runners go?
Volmari Iso-Hollo of Finland won the extra lap too, and because of the error his time was never ratified as a record.
Three Finns shared the gold medal on the same gymnastics apparatus in 1948. Which apparatus?
Paavo Aaltonen, Veikko Huhtanen and Heikki Savolainen all scored exactly the same, and Finland won the team title as well.
Finland has won Olympic boxing gold twice. Who won the second, in front of a home crowd in 1952?
Sten Suvio had won the first in Berlin in 1936, and no Finn has won boxing gold in the seventy years since.
Sylvi Saimo won an Olympic gold at Helsinki in 1952, at the age of 38. In which sport?
She is still the only Finnish woman to have won an Olympic canoeing title, and she had trained on the lake by her home.
Pentti Linnosvuo won Olympic shooting golds eight years apart. What did he use?
The free pistol at fifty metres in 1956 and the rapid-fire pistol in 1964, two events that share almost nothing but the hand.
Which Finn beat the Kenyan favourite Kipchoge Keino to the Olympic 1500 metres gold in 1972?
He stayed at the back for twelve hundred metres and then ran a final lap of about 53 seconds.
Which Finnish fireman won the Olympic single sculls at three Games in a row from 1976?
Two metres tall and rowing out of Vehmaa, he beat the East German Peter-Michael Kolbe in two of those three finals.
Finland's last two Olympic golds in men's throwing events came at the same Games. Which Games?
Juha Tiainen took the hammer and Arto Harkonen the javelin, four days apart, and no Finnish man has thrown for gold since.
Tapio Korjus won the 1988 Olympic javelin with the last throw of the competition. By what margin?
He beat Jan Zelezny, who went on to set the world record and win three Olympic titles of his own.
Heli Rantanen was the first Finnish woman to win an Olympic athletics gold. What won it for her?
The first throw of the final
She threw it in 1996 and then watched eleven rivals fail to pass it, having never won a major medal before or after.
Satu Makela-Nummela won Finland's most recent Summer Olympic gold in 2008. In which sport?
The tally has not moved since: Finland came home from London, Rio, Tokyo and Paris without a single gold medal.
Lydia Wideman won Finland's first women's Winter Olympic gold in 1952. Why not earlier?
Women had not been allowed to ski
Women's cross-country skiing was on the Olympic programme for the first time that year, as a single 10-kilometre race.
Antti Hyvarinen won Finland's first Olympic ski jumping gold in 1956. With what?
The Norwegians thought the style ugly and unsporting, and his team-mate Aulis Kallakorpi took silver with it the same day.
Marja-Liisa Hamalainen won three cross-country golds at Sarajevo in 1984. What was Finland's fourth?
Matti Nykanen won it, and Finland came away from those Games with thirteen medals in all.
Toni Nieminen set a record at the 1992 Winter Olympics that still stands. Which record?
He was sixteen years and 259 days old when he won the large hill, and no younger man has won a Winter Olympic title since.
Samppa Lajunen won three golds at Salt Lake City in 2002 and then did what?
He had won the sprint, the individual and the team Nordic combined, and quit two years later saying there was nothing left to win.
Janne Lahtela's 2002 Olympic gold was Finland's first on skis away from which two sports?
He won the moguls, and until then every Finnish Olympic skiing medal had come from the tracks or the hills.
Mika Myllyla won the Olympic cross-country gold of 1998 over which distance?
Three years later he was one of six Finns caught in the doping scandal at the Lahti world championships, and Finnish skiing never regained its standing.
Finland's first ice hockey world title, in 1995, was won in which city?
Taking it in the neighbour's own capital made the homecoming bigger than the final; a hundred thousand people filled the market square in Helsinki.
By how many goals did Finland beat Sweden in the 2011 ice hockey world championship final?
The final went 6-1, the heaviest beating in a world championship final for decades, and the tournament was played in Slovakia.
Finland won the 2019 ice hockey world championship with almost no NHL players. Whom did it beat in the final?
The squad was built out of Liiga players and young professionals, and it won 3-1 in Bratislava against a team of stars.
In which year did Finland reach an ice hockey world championship final for the first time?
It lost that final 5-2 to Sweden in Prague, and the first gold came only three years afterwards.
Finland staged an ice hockey world championship for the first time in 1965. Where?
The Soviet Union won it there, one of nine world titles it took in a row between 1963 and 1971.
Which country won nine ice hockey world championships in a row?
Nine from 1963 to 1971, and 22 world titles in all before the country ceased to exist.
The first ice hockey world championship, in 1920, was played as part of what?
A winter sport was settled at a Summer Games, indoors in April, months before the rest of the Olympic programme.
Which country won the ice hockey world championship of 1936, the only time it ever has?
Its team was built almost entirely from players raised in Canada who happened to hold British passports.
Which country broke the Soviet Union's run by winning the 1972 world championship at home in Prague?
It was the first time in ten years that the Soviet Union had not won, and the crowd would not stop singing.
Which country won its only ice hockey world championship in 2002, nine years after becoming independent?
It beat Russia 4-3 in Gothenburg with a goal in the last two minutes of the final.
Who was the first Finn to start a Formula One race, back in 1974?
His only start was the Swedish Grand Prix, in a privately entered Surtees, and he retired after eight laps.
One man on every list of Finnish Formula One drivers never started a race. Who?
He entered two Grands Prix in 1977 and failed to qualify for both, so his whole career is two entries and no laps.
How many Grands Prix did Keke Rosberg win in the season he became world champion?
One was enough in 1982, a year in which eleven different drivers won a race; he won five in his whole career.
Which Finn was ordered to let his Ferrari team-mate past while leading the 1999 German Grand Prix?
He was standing in for the injured Michael Schumacher, obeyed the order, and never won a race in 109 starts.
By how many points did Kimi Raikkonen win the Formula One world championship of 2007?
He had been seventeen points behind with two races to go, and the title was settled in the last half-hour of the season.
Heikki Kovalainen won exactly one Formula One race. Which one?
He inherited it when the leader's engine blew with three laps left; he was McLaren's second driver that season.
Nico Rosberg, son of a Finnish world champion, raced under which flag?
He was born in Wiesbaden and brought up in Monaco, and chose his German mother's country over his father's.
The first Tour de France, in 1903, was made up of how many stages?
Maurice Garin rode the 2,428 kilometres in just over 94 hours, and the race had been invented to sell newspapers.
Which rider won the overall, the climbers' and the points competitions of one Tour de France?
He did it in 1969, the first of his five wins, and nobody has taken all three in one Tour since.
Four riders have won the Tour de France five times. Which of them won five in consecutive years?
1991 to 1995; the other three spread their wins out over longer careers, and he never lost the lead once he had it.
Who was the last French rider to win the Tour de France?
He won in 1985, and no home rider has won since, by far the longest drought in the race's history.
Which Tour de France winner was shot by accident while hunting and came back to win twice more?
He took a shotgun blast in the back and side in 1987 and won the 1989 Tour by eight seconds, the narrowest margin ever.
Gino Bartali's two Tour de France wins are the furthest apart in history. How many years lie between?
He won in 1938 and 1948; the war took most of the gap, and he spent part of it smuggling forged papers in his bicycle frame.
Lance Armstrong's seven Tour de France titles were struck from the record. Who got them instead?
The organisers decided those years should simply stand empty, so the official list of winners has seven blank lines in it.
Which rider won the Giro d'Italia, the Tour de France and the world road race title all in 1987?
Only Eddy Merckx had managed the treble before him, and nobody has managed it since.
What cut short the decisive mountain stage of the 2019 Tour de France?
Hail and mud buried the road, the stage was stopped, and Egan Bernal became the first Colombian winner at the age of 22.
Bradley Wiggins was the first British winner of the Tour de France. What did he win ten days later?
The 2012 Tour finished on 22 July and the London Olympic time trial was on 1 August, which he won on home roads.
The 2006 Tour de France winner lost the title to a failed test. Who was given it instead?
He had been let into a breakaway nobody bothered to chase, gained nearly half an hour, and lost most of it again in the Alps.
Bjarne Riis admitted doping after winning the 1996 Tour de France. What is his official status?
The organisers no longer treat him as the winner, but the cycling union never changed the result, so his name is still in the record book.
Jarmila Kratochvilova's world record of 1:53.28, set in 1983, is in which event?
It is the oldest standing record in athletics; no woman has come within a second of it in more than forty years.
In which event did Marita Koch of East Germany run 47.60 in 1985?
It is still quicker than any woman has run since, and the East German records of that decade have never been struck from the books.
Mike Powell jumped 8.95 metres in Tokyo in 1991. Whose record did that beat?
Beamon's 8.90 from the thin air of Mexico City had stood for 23 years, and Carl Lewis jumped 8.91 in the same competition with too much wind.
Javier Sotomayor's high jump world record of 2.45 m has stood since 1993. How tall is he?
So he cleared half a metre above his own head, and no one has matched the bar in over thirty years.
Jonathan Edwards broke the triple jump world record twice in 1995. How far apart?
He jumped 18.16 and then 18.29 in consecutive attempts at the Gothenburg world championships, and the second still stands.
Why has nobody thrown a javelin 100 metres?
The javelin was redesigned to fly shorter
In 1986 the centre of gravity was moved forward so that throws would stop landing among the spectators; the record with the new spear is 98.48 m.
Yuriy Sedykh set a world record in 1986 that still stands. In which event?
86.74 metres, and no hammer thrower in forty years has come within a metre of it.
Florence Griffith Joyner's 100 metres record of 10.49 has been argued over ever since. Why?
Nearby gauges at the 1988 US trials showed a strong tailwind while hers showed none, and the mark has stood for nearly forty years.
Usain Bolt ran 9.58 for 100 metres in 2009. At which championships?
He took eleven hundredths off his own record, the biggest single improvement since electronic timing began.
Which country's runner has held the men's 1500 metres world record since 1998?
Hicham El Guerrouj ran 3:26.00 in Rome, having fallen in two Olympic finals before he finally won in Athens in 2004.
The women's shot put world record of 22.63 m dates from which decade?
Natalya Lisovskaya set it in 1987, and no woman has thrown within a metre of it since.
Jackie Joyner-Kersee's heptathlon world record has stood since which year?
She scored 7291 points at the Seoul Olympics, and nobody since has come within 200 points of it.
The men's 4x400 metres relay world record has stood since 1993. Which country set it?
The four men averaged about 43.6 seconds each, with Michael Johnson running the anchor leg in Stuttgart.
The 1908 Olympic marathon fixed the distance still run today. What decided the odd 385 yards?
The position of the Royal Box
The runners entered the stadium opposite the box and the direction of running was reversed so the finish could be seen from it, leaving 385 yards instead of a full lap.
Where did the 1908 Olympic marathon start?
It began on the path beside the castle's East Lawn and finished in front of the Royal Box at White City, 26 miles and 385 yards later.
In which year was 42.195 km made the official marathon distance?
Thirteen years after the London race it copies, and the governing body never properly explained why that particular course was chosen.
Dorando Pietri crossed the line first in the 1908 Olympic marathon. Why was he not the winner?
He had run the wrong way
He was over the age limit
He collapsed five times inside the stadium and umpires lifted him each time; he was disqualified, and Queen Alexandra gave him a cup the next day instead.
The 1896 Olympic marathon was run over what distance?
The distance changed from Games to Games until 1921, so the early winners' times cannot be compared with anything.
Which of these is NOT one of boxing's original eight weight divisions?
The traditional eight are flyweight, bantamweight, featherweight, lightweight, welterweight, middleweight, light heavyweight and heavyweight; the rest were added after the 1960s.
How many professional boxing weight divisions are recognised today?
Eighteen have a ceiling and heavyweight has none; there were eight until the governing bodies split and began inventing super and junior classes.
Which boxing division did the WBC invent in 2020, between cruiserweight and heavyweight?
Its ceiling is 224 pounds, the WBA calls it super cruiserweight, and hardly anyone fights in it.
In how many of boxing's original eight divisions did Manny Pacquiao win world titles?
Flyweight, featherweight, lightweight and welterweight, a span of 35 pounds, which is about sixteen kilos of the same man.
Which American law of 1920 gave boxing its standard weight limits?
It set up the New York State Athletic Commission; before 1909 sources could not even agree what counted as a light weight.
Which sport was an Olympic event at six Games up to 1920 and has never come back?
It ran from 1900 to 1920, and in 1908 British police teams took all three medals between them.
Which of these has genuinely been an Olympic sport?
Paris 1900 only; every competitor was French and the crowd is said to have consisted of one paying spectator.
Which contest handed out Olympic medals from 1912 to 1948 without any sport being played?
There were medals for painting, sculpture, architecture, literature and music on sporting themes, and Pierre de Coubertin won a literature gold under a pseudonym.
Which swimming event, held once in 1904, was won without swimming a stroke?
Competitors dived in and glided face down, motionless, and whoever drifted furthest won; the sport was judged too dull to repeat.
Which motorised sport awarded Olympic medals in 1908?
It is the only time engines have competed for Olympic medals, and the weather was so bad that in two of the three races only one boat finished.
Which gymnastics event was an Olympic sport five times, the last in 1932?
It was contested in 1896, 1904, 1906, 1924 and 1932, judged on speed and, in the early years, on style as well.
Which cycling event, raced by two riders on one bicycle, left the Olympics after 1972?
Two men on one bike over 2000 metres, in and out of the programme since 1906, and gone for good when the track events were reorganised.
Which swimming event was in the Olympics in 1984, 1988 and 1992 and then dropped?
A judged sport with no opponent in the pool at all; the duet and the team event survived, the soloist did not.
Which of these was an Olympic athletics event before 1913?
The standing high, long and triple jumps were all contested up to 1912, and the American Ray Ewry won eight golds in them.
Which team sport was in the Olympics only in 1936, played eleven a side on a full-sized field?
Germany won it at home in front of a huge crowd; the indoor seven-a-side version replaced it when handball returned in 1972.
Which sport was an Olympic event five times, the last in 1936, and is played on horseback?
It appeared in 1900, 1908, 1920, 1924 and 1936, and Argentina won the last two tournaments.
Which equestrian events were contested at the 1900 Olympics and never again?
Horses jumped for height and distance as athletes do, and both events disappeared after one outing in Paris.
Which old French racket game, played off the walls indoors, was an Olympic sport in 1908?
Real tennis, the game lawn tennis descends from; it appeared once and has never returned.
Which two bat-and-ball sports were dropped after 2008 and brought back for one Games in 2021?
The Tokyo organisers were allowed to add sports of local interest, and both went out again straight afterwards.
Which Grand Slam complex is named after a First World War fighter pilot?
Roland Garros was an aviator who died in 1918 and had nothing to do with tennis; a friend who ran the club insisted on the name.
Which Grand Slam show court was the first to get a retractable roof?
Melbourne built it in 1988, two decades before Wimbledon; the city's heat was as much the reason as its rain.
Which Grand Slam has the largest main stadium?
Arthur Ashe Stadium holds about 23,000, against roughly 15,000 at Centre Court and 14,800 at Rod Laver Arena.
The US Open is played on the site of what?
Flushing Meadows hosted the World's Fairs of 1939 and 1964, and the park was built on what had been an ash dump.
Which club has won more Finnish ice hockey championships than any other?
Twenty-one in all, fourteen of them since the league turned professional in 1975, and it plays in Tampere.
Which Finnish club has sixteen championships but has won only one since 1975?
Fifteen of its titles came before the SM-liiga existed, and its last one was in 1985.
Which club won five Finnish championships and no longer plays in the Liiga at all?
Four titles in the 1990s and one in 2002, and then it left for the Russian league in 2014.
Lukko of Rauma has won two Finnish championships. How far apart are they?
The first came in 1963 and the second in 2021, which is a long time to keep a town hoping.
Which club won four Finnish ice hockey championships in five years from 2004?
It won again in 2014, 2015 and 2018, making eight titles in fifteen years for a city of 200,000.
Which club has won the Finnish championship exactly twice, in 2006 and in 2019?
It won in 2006 and 2019, and both times it had finished the regular season well down the table.
Which club won its first ever Finnish ice hockey championship in 2025?
The club had been playing since the 1920s and had reached a final only once before.
Which Liiga club plays in a rink still called a sports park, Kisapuisto?
It is in Lappeenranta, it is the smallest ground in the league, and the club has never won the championship.
Which club has won the Finnish championship in 2009 and 2012 and at no other time?
They are its only two titles, and in between it beat several KHL clubs in European competition.
What do the letters HS stand for on a modern ski jumping hill?
It is the distance from the take-off to the point where the landing slope flattens out too much to land on safely, and it replaced the K-point as the figure everyone quotes.
How large must a hill be before it counts as a ski flying hill?
There are only five certified ski flying hills in the world, in Austria, Germany, Norway, Slovenia and the Czech Republic.
Which is the largest ski jumping hill in Finland?
At HS 142 it is bigger than Lahti and Kuopio, both HS 130, and Finland has no ski flying hill at all.
Two hills in the world are built to HS 240. One is Vikersund in Norway. Where is the other?
The two share the title of largest hill on earth, and every world record jump of recent decades has been made on one of them.
The Lahti ski jumping hills are named Salpausselka. What is a Salpausselka?
The ridges were pushed up at the edge of the retreating ice sheet, and the jumps are built on the side of one of them.
Which of Finland's main ski jumping hills is the smallest?
At HS 97 it is a normal hill rather than a large one, which makes it the furthest north and the least used in competition.
Which country has the largest hill in the world that is not a ski flying hill?
The Muhlenkopfschanze at Willingen is HS 147, and the World Cup event there regularly draws crowds of forty thousand.
What is the largest stadium in the world by capacity?
The Narendra Modi Stadium in Ahmedabad holds 132,000, some 33,000 more than Camp Nou, the biggest football-only ground.
Which sport accounts for most of the ten largest stadiums on earth?
Eight of the top ten are university grounds in the United States, several of them in towns smaller than Porvoo.
Which is the largest stadium in Europe?
It holds 99,354 in Barcelona; Wembley at 90,000 is second in Europe, the Bernabeu third and Croke Park in Dublin fourth.
Which country has the world's second largest stadium, holding over 113,000?
The Rungrado 1st of May Stadium in Pyongyang is used for mass gymnastic displays as much as for football.
Nearly 200,000 people saw the 1950 World Cup decider at the Maracana. What does it hold now?
Seating and safety rules have cut it by more than half; the 1950 crowd remains the largest ever at a football match.
Which is the largest stadium in the southern hemisphere?
It holds 100,024 and is used for cricket in summer and Australian rules football in winter.
The Finnish men's football team is called Huuhkajat. What is a huuhkaja?
One flew onto the pitch during a Finland-Belgium match in 2007, stopped play, Finland won, and the bird gave the team its name.
Finland's women's football team is known as Helmarit. What does the name mean?
It blends helmi, a pearl, with huuhkaja, the eagle owl of the men's team, and was chosen by a public vote.
Which country's football team has been called the Wunderteam since the 1930s?
The name came from a fourteen-match unbeaten run under Hugo Meisl, and it has outlived the team's success by ninety years.
Why was the Dutch football team of the 1970s called Clockwork Orange?
A pun on the film title, applied to a side so well drilled that it reached two World Cup finals and lost both.
Italy's football team is Gli Azzurri, the Blues. Where does the blue come from?
It is the colour of the royal family's coat of arms, and Italy kept it long after it stopped being a monarchy.
England's nickname, the Three Lions, comes from a coat of arms first recorded in which century?
The three lions appear on a royal seal of 1198, so the badge is some seven hundred years older than the football association.
Which country's football team is nicknamed Drillos, after a man rather than a symbol?
Egil Olsen, known as Drillo, managed the team in the 1990s and his nickname attached itself to the whole side.
Portugal's team is the Selecao das Quinas. What are the quinas?
Shields on the coat of arms
They are the five small shields arranged on the national arms, each bearing five dots, and the national team is named after them rather than a colour or an animal.
What does Croatia's football nickname Vatreni mean?
Vatra means fire; the team is also called Kockasti, the chequered ones, after the red and white squares on the shirt.
Switzerland's football team is simply called Nati. What is that short for?
It is the German for national team, used in a country with four official languages because no better compromise was found.
Which decade gave the Danish football team the nickname Danish Dynamite?
The side of Elkjaer and Laudrup played thrilling football, were everyone's second favourite team, and won nothing at all.
Football's back-pass rule arrived in 1992. Which tournament had made it necessary?
It was widely called the dullest World Cup ever played, full of back-passes and goalkeepers standing on the ball to run the clock down.
Despite its name, football's back-pass rule applies to a pass in which direction?
What matters is that a team-mate deliberately kicked it to the keeper, not where on the pitch either of them was standing.
A keeper may not pick up a team-mate's deliberate kick. What about a deliberate header?
He must let it go out
The laws define a kick as using the foot, so head, chest, shin and knee are all fine; but a defender may not flick the ball up on purpose to get round the rule.
What is the punishment for a goalkeeper breaking the back-pass rule?
It is taken where the handling happened, or from the nearest point on the six-yard line if that was inside the six-yard box.
In 1997 the back-pass rule was extended to cover the ball reaching the keeper from what?
The first season under the original rule had shown that teams were simply throwing the ball to the goalkeeper instead of kicking it.
In which year did the NBA introduce the 24-second shot clock?
Teams had been sitting on the ball once ahead; one game in 1950 finished 19-18, and the clock roughly doubled scoring within a few seasons.
Until 1938, what happened in basketball after every single basket?
Play restarted with a jump ball in the middle every time, which is why tall men who could do nothing else still had a job.
Dribbling was allowed in basketball from 1901, but with what restriction?
You could not use your left hand
You could not move your feet
Only one bounce was permitted and the dribble had to end in a pass; the modern continuous dribble was legalised in 1909.
In Naismith's original rules, what happened if one side committed three fouls in a row?
The opponents were given a goal
Fouls meant striking, holding, pushing or tripping; three in a row and the other side simply had a point written down.
In the original basketball rules a goal counted only if the ball did what?
Was thrown from outside the circle
So after every score somebody had to fetch the ball out again, which is also why the game was slower than it looks on paper.
Naismith's rules banned punching the ball. What was allowed instead?
Batting it with an open hand
The ball could be thrown or batted in any direction with one hand or both, but never struck with a fist.
Goaltending, swatting away a shot on its way down, became a basketball foul in which year?
It had been perfectly legal for the first half-century of the game; offensive goaltending followed only in 1958.
The NBA added a restricted-zone arc under the basket in 1997 to stop what?
Defenders standing there to draw charges
A defender could park himself under the basket and collect a foul every time an attacker landed on him; FIBA copied the idea in 2010 with a smaller arc.
How long were the two halves in basketball's original rules?
Fifteen minutes each with five minutes' rest, and a throw-in had to be taken within five seconds, a limit that has survived everything else.
